case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a U.S. federal district court has subject-matter jurisdiction to criminally prosecute a foreign state’s instrumentality (a state-owned bank) under 18 U.S.C. § 3231, or whether the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA) and related common-law principles instead bar such criminal proceedings absent a clear statement from Congress.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 3231 (federal criminal jurisdiction); Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1441(d), 1602–1611 (sovereign immunity framework).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Halkbank argues that as an instrumentality of a foreign sovereign it is immune from U.S. criminal prosecution unless Congress clearly abrogated that immunity; it contends the FSIA is the exclusive, comprehensive scheme governing foreign-sovereign immunity and jurisdiction in U.S. courts, and because the FSIA is framed around civil actions and does not clearly authorize criminal prosecutions of foreign states or their instrumentalities, federal courts lack subject-matter jurisdiction (or must recognize immunity) notwithstanding the general criminal-jurisdiction grant in § 3231. Petitioner and supporting amici also invoke background principles of international law and the historical presumption that general jurisdictional statutes do not silently include foreign sovereigns (often associated with The Schooner Exchange tradition), warning that allowing criminal prosecutions would create serious reciprocal and diplomatic consequences for states and state-owned enterprises.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues the FSIA does not provide blanket immunity from criminal proceedings and is primarily a civil immunity/jurisdiction statute; nothing in the FSIA withdraws the district courts’ preexisting criminal jurisdiction under § 3231. On that view, foreign state-owned enterprises can be prosecuted when federal criminal statutes apply to their conduct (especially where the case concerns alleged evasion of U.S. sanctions and U.S.-connected financial activity), and immunity questions should not be inferred from the FSIA’s civil-text structure to negate criminal jurisdiction.
key_precedents: In re Grand Jury, 912 F.3d 623 (D.C. Cir.)
The Schooner Exchange v. McFaddon, 11 U.S. (7 Cranch) 116 (1812)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s clear-statement/sovereign-immunity baseline (The Schooner Exchange) is the best argument for petitioner, but I do not think FSIA § 1604’s general reference to being “immune from the jurisdiction of the courts” can be read—against the Act’s persistent “civil action” architecture—to silently retract § 3231’s separate, unqualified criminal-jurisdiction grant over “all offenses.” Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch are persuasive that Verlinden and Amerada Hess speak to FSIA exclusivity in the civil context, and Samantar cautions against extending the FSIA beyond its scope; those precedents support a restrained holding that jurisdiction exists while leaving any residual immunity questions (if any) to common-law analysis on a properly developed record. Under my minimalist approach, the narrow path that best preserves institutional legitimacy is to avoid announcing categorical criminal immunity by implication and instead decide only that FSIA does not divest § 3231 jurisdiction in criminal prosecutions. If an instrumentality has a viable immunity defense, it should be addressed directly and narrowly rather than by converting statutory silence into a sweeping jurisdictional bar.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The strongest opposing point—pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito—is that § 3231’s grant over “all offenses” is clear and the FSIA’s civil-focused machinery makes it an implausible vehicle to withdraw criminal jurisdiction. But that response never squarely answers the antecedent originalist question: absent a clear congressional statement, the background rule recognized in The Schooner Exchange is that foreign sovereigns and their instrumentalities are not amenable to a court’s coercive jurisdiction, and FSIA § 1604 codifies that immunity in jurisdictional terms (“immune from the jurisdiction of the courts”) without carving out criminal proceedings. Samantar does not help respondents: if the FSIA’s detailed scheme is limited to civil actions, that limitation does not create a judicial power to proceed criminally; it restores the pre-FSIA baseline immunity rather than negating it, and under a textualist clear-statement rule I will not treat § 3231’s general grant as impliedly abrogating sovereign immunity. Because Congress has not spoken with the requisite clarity to subject foreign sovereign instrumentalities to federal criminal process, I would hold the prosecution barred for want of jurisdiction.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s clear-statement point, grounded in The Schooner Exchange and his reading of FSIA § 1604 as a jurisdictional bar, is the most serious objection, but it still does not supply the statutory clarity needed to negate Congress’s unqualified criminal-jurisdiction grant in § 3231 over “all offenses.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the FSIA’s text and machinery are calibrated to “civil action[s]” (e.g., § 1330(a)’s “nonjury civil action” and civil service/pleading provisions), making it implausible—on a textualist reading—to treat § 1604 as silently withdrawing criminal jurisdiction. Verlinden/Amerada Hess’s “sole basis” language is best confined to the civil context those cases decided, and Samantar cuts against extending the FSIA beyond its scope by implication; at most, any residual immunity would have to be argued as a common-law defense, not a jurisdictional nullification of § 3231. Practical consequences reinforce this reading: Thomas’s approach would create an immunity-by-silence loophole for state-owned commercial entities to commit U.S.-connected crimes absent an FSIA exception Congress never drafted for criminal cases.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to insist that The Schooner Exchange reflects a deep background principle and that we should hesitate before finding a “momentous” abrogation of immunity by implication, but that principle cuts in favor of demanding clarity in the direction he proposes—reading a civil-focused statute to withdraw criminal jurisdiction would itself be an implied, not clear, limitation on § 3231. As Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice emphasize, the FSIA’s operative design is repeatedly and deliberately keyed to “civil action[s]” and civil procedure, so § 1604’s general phrase cannot sensibly be read to silently negate Congress’s unqualified criminal-jurisdiction grant over “all offenses.” Samantar matters here: if the FSIA does not cover criminal prosecutions, the consequence is not a jurisdictional void but that any residual immunity (if it exists) must be assessed through common-law doctrines rather than by expanding FSIA beyond its scope. Given the real-world enforcement gap Thomas’s reading would create for state-owned commercial actors, I would hold § 3231 confers jurisdiction and reject treating FSIA silence as categorical criminal immunity.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s clearest point is the Schooner Exchange baseline and the related clear-statement instinct: if immunity is a jurisdictional limit, Congress must speak plainly before exposing foreign sovereign instrumentalities to criminal process. But the enacted text cuts the other way—FSIA’s operative architecture is built around “civil action[s]” (as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch stress), so reading § 1604’s general “immune from the jurisdiction” clause to silently retract § 3231’s distinct criminal-jurisdiction grant over “all offenses” is an implausible fit and looks like repeal-by-implication. Samantar, which Thomas invokes, actually reinforces the scope-bound approach: when the FSIA doesn’t cover a category, we don’t expand the statute; any residual immunity arguments belong (if anywhere) in common-law doctrine, not as a subject-matter jurisdiction negation. Pragmatically and textually, the workable coherent rule is jurisdiction under § 3231, with any immunity claim addressed separately rather than converting FSIA silence into categorical criminal immunity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press the Schooner Exchange baseline and the clear-statement concern, and I take seriously his reading of § 1604’s “immune from the jurisdiction” language as jurisdictional in character. But text and structure still matter: as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, the FSIA’s operative provisions are relentlessly keyed to “civil action[s]” (e.g., § 1330(a), § 1441(d), service/answer mechanics), making it methodologically unsound to treat § 1604 as an implied repeal of § 3231’s separate, unqualified criminal-jurisdiction grant over “all offenses.” Verlinden and Amerada Hess’s “sole basis” language (noted by Justice Roberts) was issued in the civil posture the FSIA was designed to address, and under our separation-of-powers traditions I will not extend that dicta to negate Congress’s criminal jurisdiction absent a clear, on-point statutory command. If immunity remains for foreign instrumentalities in criminal prosecutions, Samantar’s framework (highlighted by Justice Kagan) points to a common-law merits defense, not a jurisdictional bar that nullifies § 3231.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s clear-statement argument, rooted in The Schooner Exchange and his reading of FSIA § 1604’s “immune from the jurisdiction” language, is the strongest case for Petitioner, but it runs into the FSIA’s enacted structure that is explicitly calibrated to “civil action[s]” (as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize). Given § 3231’s unqualified grant over “all offenses,” I do not see a legitimate textual basis to treat the FSIA—through a civil-focused immunity provision and civil procedural machinery—as silently retracting criminal subject-matter jurisdiction Congress plainly conferred. Roberts’s point about Verlinden/Amerada Hess being civil-context “sole basis” statements, together with Samantar’s caution against extending the FSIA beyond its scope, reinforces the institutionalist, precedent-respecting course: hold that § 3231 jurisdiction exists and leave any residual immunity questions (if any) to common-law analysis rather than an implied jurisdictional repeal. On practical and legitimacy grounds, I also agree with Justice Alito that an immunity-by-silence rule would create a substantial enforcement gap Congress did not clearly command.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas is right to press the clear-statement principle rooted in The Schooner Exchange and echoed in FSIA § 1604’s broad phrase “immune from the jurisdiction,” but the best textual reading is that § 1604’s jurisdictional bar operates within the FSIA’s own civil-action framework rather than as a freestanding limitation on all federal judicial power. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, the FSIA’s structure repeatedly cabins its operative provisions to “civil action[s]” (e.g., § 1330(a), § 1441(d), and service/answer provisions), making it difficult to treat the Act as silently withdrawing § 3231’s unqualified grant over “all offenses against the laws of the United States.” Samantar strengthens that conclusion: where the FSIA does not apply, we do not expand the statute by implication; any residual immunity must be analyzed under whatever common-law doctrine exists, not by negating subject-matter jurisdiction. I therefore would affirm jurisdiction under § 3231 while leaving any properly presented common-law immunity defense for separate consideration.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s clear-statement point, grounded in The Schooner Exchange and his reading of FSIA § 1604 as jurisdictional, is the hardest push against my view; but the statute Congress enacted is structurally and procedurally built for “civil action[s],” making it an implausible vehicle for silently retracting § 3231’s categorical criminal-jurisdiction grant over “all offenses.” Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively connect Samantar to the proper limiting principle: when the FSIA does not cover a category (here, federal criminal prosecutions), we do not convert statutory silence into a jurisdictional bar; at most we consider any residual immunity under common-law doctrines without negating subject-matter jurisdiction. From a pragmatic, fairness-focused perspective, treating FSIA’s civil immunity framework as implied criminal immunity would create an enforcement gap and procedural unpredictability Congress did not design. I therefore continue to read § 3231 as controlling on jurisdiction, with any immunity arguments addressed through the correct, narrower doctrinal channel rather than by expanding the FSIA beyond its civil domain.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3231 grants the district courts original jurisdiction over "all offenses against the laws of the United States," and nothing in the FSIA’s text withdraws that criminal jurisdiction or creates a clear immunity bar in criminal cases. Verlinden held that the FSIA is the "sole basis" for obtaining jurisdiction over a foreign state in civil actions, but that holding does not, on its own terms, displace § 3231 or supply a clear-statement rule against criminal enforcement absent express congressional abrogation. Consistent with Samantar, where the FSIA does not apply, any immunity question remains a matter of federal common law, and we should avoid a broad, institutionally disruptive ruling that would immunize state-owned commercial entities from generally applicable federal criminal statutes. A narrow disposition is to affirm subject-matter jurisdiction under § 3231 and leave any residual immunity arguments to be addressed under applicable common-law principles rather than by expanding the FSIA beyond its civil framework.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Section 3231’s general grant of criminal jurisdiction should not be read to reach foreign sovereigns or their instrumentalities absent a clear statement, given the longstanding background rule reflected in The Schooner Exchange that sovereign immunity limits the courts’ jurisdiction. The FSIA’s text confirms that baseline: § 1604 provides that a “foreign state shall be immune from the jurisdiction of the courts of the United States” unless a statutory exception applies, and the Act’s operative jurisdictional/exception provisions (e.g., § 1330(a)) are framed around “civil action[s],” not criminal prosecutions. Reading the FSIA as the comprehensive scheme Congress enacted in 1976, and applying a strict textualist clear-statement principle for abrogating sovereign immunity, I would hold that Congress has not clearly authorized criminal prosecution of a foreign state instrumentality here. Because immunity is jurisdictional in character under the FSIA’s structure, the district court lacks authority to proceed absent a clearly applicable FSIA exception or express criminal abrogation.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 3231 gives district courts “original jurisdiction ... of all offenses against the laws of the United States,” and its text contains no carveout for foreign sovereigns or their instrumentalities; “all means all,” so the court has subject-matter jurisdiction over a federal criminal prosecution. The FSIA’s text and structure are aimed at civil actions (e.g., §§ 1330, 1441(d), 1604) and do not clearly withdraw or limit the criminal-jurisdiction grant Congress made in § 3231; absent an express statutory displacement, we should not infer one. While we have said in the civil context that the FSIA is the “sole basis” for jurisdiction over a foreign state, that statement (from Amerada Hess) does not transform a civil immunity/jurisdiction scheme into a bar on criminal prosecutions where Congress has separately conferred jurisdiction and where practical consequences counsel against creating an immunity loophole for state-owned enterprises engaging in U.S.-connected criminal conduct. Any immunity beyond the FSIA’s terms would have to come from a clear congressional statement or established common-law rule, and neither defeats § 3231’s straightforward jurisdictional command here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 3231 plainly grants district courts jurisdiction over “all offenses against the laws of the United States,” and nothing in the FSIA’s text withdraws that criminal jurisdiction. The FSIA is structured and worded as a civil framework—conferring jurisdiction over “nonjury civil action[s]” under 28 U.S.C. § 1330(a) and prescribing civil procedures like service and “answer” deadlines in §§ 1608(d) and 1441(d)—so it is a poor fit to infer a categorical criminal immunity bar absent an express provision. Under Samantar v. Yousuf, 560 U.S. 305 (2010), the FSIA does not displace all immunity questions outside its scope; but that leaves, at most, a common-law immunity inquiry, not a subject-matter jurisdiction defect that overrides § 3231. Given the strong public interest in enforcing criminal laws against U.S.-connected financial and sanctions-evasion conduct, I would not create a broad, judge-made immunity for state-owned commercial instrumentalities without a clear directive from Congress.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3231 confers subject-matter jurisdiction over "all offenses against the laws of the United States," and nothing in the FSIA’s text clearly withdraws that longstanding criminal-jurisdiction grant. The FSIA is framed as a comprehensive scheme for civil "actions" against "foreign states" (28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1602–1611), and under ordinary textual inference a civil immunity/jurisdiction statute should not be read to impliedly bar federal criminal prosecutions absent a clear statement. Samantar confirms that the FSIA’s exclusivity is limited to the category it addresses and that immunity questions outside its scope may be governed by common law, 560 U.S. at 325—so the absence of an FSIA criminal-immunity rule does not negate § 3231 jurisdiction. Workability also favors allowing prosecution where Congress has criminalized the conduct of “whoever” and where the entity operates commercially; any immunity limitation should come from Congress, not an implied carveout from a civil statute.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 3231 confers subject-matter jurisdiction over “all offenses against the laws of the United States,” and nothing in its text excludes foreign states or their instrumentalities, so a federal court’s criminal jurisdiction is not displaced absent a clear congressional command. The FSIA’s operative provisions are framed in civil terms—e.g., jurisdiction over “any nonjury civil action” in 28 U.S.C. § 1330(a) and removal of “any civil action” in § 1441(d)—and its silence about criminal prosecutions is best read as leaving preexisting criminal jurisdiction under § 3231 untouched rather than silently creating a new criminal immunity. Verlinden confirms the FSIA supplies the governing rules “in every action against a foreign sovereign” within its scope, but it does not suggest the statute withdraws criminal jurisdiction where Congress has separately granted it, and Samantar underscores that immunity questions outside the FSIA’s coverage may proceed under common law only where that law actually supplies an immunity. Whatever residual common-law immunity may exist, the better separation-of-powers course is not to infer a categorical criminal immunity that Congress did not enact, especially where Congress has broadly made federal criminal laws applicable to “persons” and provided district courts jurisdiction to adjudicate offenses.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Section 3231 confers broad subject-matter jurisdiction on federal district courts over “all offenses against the laws of the United States,” and nothing in the FSIA’s text clearly withdraws that longstanding criminal jurisdiction. The FSIA is framed as a civil jurisdiction/immunity scheme (e.g., 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1604–1607) and this Court has treated it as comprehensive in the civil context, but not as silently displacing other authorities in distinct settings absent clear statutory direction. Consistent with judicial restraint and practical workability, I would not infer a criminal-prosecution immunity carveout from the FSIA’s civil-focused structure, especially where Congress has enacted generally applicable criminal statutes and § 3231 supplies jurisdiction. Verlinden confirms Congress’s primacy in this area but does not itself establish that the FSIA extends to, or bars, federal criminal prosecutions of foreign instrumentalities.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Section 3231’s text grants district courts jurisdiction over “all offenses against the laws of the United States,” and nothing in that provision carves out foreign sovereign instrumentalities. The FSIA’s text is framed as a civil scheme—granting jurisdiction in “any nonjury civil action” (§ 1330(a)) and addressing removal of “civil action[s]” (§ 1441(d))—and thus does not clearly withdraw otherwise-existing criminal jurisdiction under § 3231. While clear-statement rules counsel caution in treating sovereigns as “persons” (Vermont Agency of Natural Resources v. United States ex rel. Stevens, 529 U.S. 765 (2000)), that presumption does not transform a civil immunity/jurisdiction statute into an implied bar on criminal prosecutions absent textual indication. Consistent with In re Grand Jury, 912 F.3d 623 (D.C. Cir.), the better reading is that FSIA immunity does not extend categorically to federal criminal process against foreign instrumentalities, so subject-matter jurisdiction exists under § 3231.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: 18 U.S.C. § 3231 plainly grants federal district courts jurisdiction over “all offenses against the laws of the United States,” and nothing in the FSIA’s text—structured around “civil action[s]” and civil jurisdictional grants (28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1602–1611)—clearly withdraws that criminal jurisdiction for prosecutions under generally applicable federal criminal statutes. While Halkbank invokes a clear-statement rule grounded in foreign-relations concerns and The Schooner Exchange tradition, Congress’s chosen scheme in the FSIA does not squarely address criminal prosecutions, so it cannot be read to impliedly negate § 3231’s broad jurisdictional command. Under Samantar v. Yousuf, when the FSIA does not govern a particular immunity question, courts may look to common-law immunity principles, but that analysis is distinct from—rather than a negation of—subject-matter jurisdiction under § 3231. On a pragmatic view attentive to practical consequences and procedural fairness, allowing the criminal case to proceed subject to any properly raised immunity defense avoids creating an immunity-by-silence regime that could frustrate enforcement of federal criminal law in U.S.-connected conduct.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a U.S. federal district court has subject-matter jurisdiction to criminally prosecute a foreign state’s instrumentality (a state-owned bank) under 18 U.S.C. § 3231, or whether the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (and related common-law principles) bars such prosecutions absent a clear statutory statement.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act (FSIA), 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1441(d), 1602–1611; and general federal criminal jurisdiction statute, 18 U.S.C. § 3231.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Halkbank argues that foreign sovereigns and their instrumentalities are presumptively immune from U.S. court jurisdiction, including in criminal cases, unless Congress clearly abrogates that immunity. It contends the FSIA supplies the exclusive, comprehensive scheme governing when foreign states and their agencies/instrumentalities may be haled into U.S. courts, and because the FSIA is structured around civil actions and contains no clear authorization for criminal prosecution of foreign sovereign instrumentalities, § 3231’s general grant of criminal jurisdiction cannot be read to override immunity. On this view, allowing criminal prosecutions based on § 3231 alone would circumvent the FSIA’s carefully calibrated exceptions and undermine international comity and reciprocity concerns emphasized by amici foreign states.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues that the FSIA does not confer blanket immunity from criminal proceedings and is principally a civil jurisdiction/immunity statute; it neither mentions criminal prosecutions nor purports to strip the federal courts of their ordinary criminal jurisdiction. Because § 3231 gives district courts jurisdiction over federal crimes, and because Congress has enacted criminal statutes that apply to entities like banks (including foreign-owned ones) when they engage in prohibited conduct with U.S. nexus, the prosecution may proceed. The government’s framing treats the FSIA as not applicable (or at least not dispositive) in the criminal context, so there is no need for a separate, explicit FSIA-style exception before a sovereign-owned corporation can be indicted under generally applicable criminal laws.
key_precedents: In re Grand Jury, 912 F.3d 623 (D.C. Cir. 2019)
The Schooner Exchange v. McFaddon, 11 U.S. (7 Cranch) 116 (1812)

John Roberts.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the background presumption of sovereign immunity (The Schooner Exchange) coupled with our “comprehensive/sole basis” language in Verlinden and Amerada Hess, but that cannot silently withdraw Congress’s unqualified criminal jurisdiction in 18 U.S.C. § 3231 without a clear statement. Justice Kagan persuasively grounds Verlinden/Amerada Hess in the civil end-run context, which makes a narrow holding both faithful to precedent and institutionally prudent: the FSIA’s repeated limitation to “nonjury civil action[s]” does not by its terms govern criminal prosecutions. Justice Thomas’s textual point—that FSIA’s civil procedures and definitions are an awkward fit for criminal process—reinforces that we should not manufacture a categorical criminal-immunity regime by implication. Consistent with minimalism, we can decide only that FSIA does not strip § 3231 jurisdiction here, leaving any residual common-law/comity immunity questions for a case that squarely presents them.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument—that the FSIA was intended to be “comprehensive” and thus displace all preexisting sovereign-immunity rules, including in criminal matters—cannot overcome the enacted text, which repeatedly limits the statute to “nonjury civil action[s]” and civil process. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito stress, 18 U.S.C. § 3231 confers jurisdiction over “all offenses,” and nothing in the FSIA contains a clear statement withdrawing that grant or creating criminal immunity for foreign-state instrumentalities. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Samantar supports, rather than undermines, this view: where FSIA does not apply by its terms, any residual immunity questions sound in common-law/comity principles, not in an implied jurisdictional repeal of § 3231. Verlinden and Amerada Hess’s “sole basis” language arose in the civil context and cannot be extended to criminal prosecutions without abandoning textualism and original public meaning.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument—rooted in The Schooner Exchange and the claim that Verlinden/Amerada Hess make the FSIA the “sole basis” for jurisdiction—still fails because it would require us to treat a statute written for “nonjury civil action[s]” as silently withdrawing 18 U.S.C. § 3231’s unqualified criminal jurisdiction over “all offenses.” Chief Justice Roberts’s clear-statement point is decisive under a textualist approach: if Congress meant to create categorical criminal immunity for foreign instrumentalities, it needed to say so, and the FSIA does not. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Samantar further confirms we should not extend the FSIA beyond its civil terms; whatever residual common-law comity exists cannot negate a clear statutory grant of criminal jurisdiction. Reading the FSIA to bar prosecutions by implication would create a serious enforcement gap in generally applicable criminal laws without any textual warrant.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains the background presumption of sovereign immunity (The Schooner Exchange) coupled with our statements that the FSIA is “comprehensive,” but that presumption cannot be used to manufacture a categorical criminal-immunity regime where Congress repeatedly spoke only of “nonjury civil action[s].” Chief Justice Roberts’s clear-statement framing is especially persuasive here: we should not treat a civil statute as silently repealing or carving back § 3231’s unqualified grant of jurisdiction over “all offenses,” because that would create a significant accountability gap with no textual anchor. Justice Kagan’s reminder that Verlinden and Amerada Hess involved civil end-runs around the FSIA underscores that their exclusivity language should not be extended to criminal prosecutions by implication. Comity and fairness concerns—especially where vulnerable communities can be harmed by misconduct—can be handled through narrower common-law and executive-branch tools, rather than by erecting a broad jurisdictional bar that Congress did not enact.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The petitioner’s best point remains the FSIA’s “comprehensive/sole basis” language in Verlinden and Amerada Hess coupled with The Schooner Exchange presumption, but those precedents were resolving civil plaintiffs’ attempts to bypass a statute drafted around “nonjury civil action[s]” and civil process—not criminal prosecutions. As Chief Justice Roberts stresses, it would take a clear statement to read a civil-focused immunity statute as silently withdrawing § 3231’s broad criminal jurisdiction over “all offenses,” and the FSIA contains no such textual hook. Justice Barrett’s emphasis on the FSIA’s civil machinery reinforces that a criminal-immunity regime by implication is textually and structurally awkward. Consistent with Samantar (as I noted and Justice Thomas echoed), where the FSIA does not apply by its terms, any residual sovereign-immunity/comity concerns should be handled through common-law or executive-branch tools rather than by inferring an unexpressed jurisdictional repeal.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains the background presumption of foreign sovereign immunity (The Schooner Exchange) coupled with the claim that Congress meant the FSIA to be comprehensive, but that cannot overcome the enacted statutory text and structure. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Thomas emphasize, the FSIA repeatedly and deliberately regulates “nonjury civil action[s]” and supplies civil-process machinery; it contains no clear statement withdrawing 18 U.S.C. § 3231’s unqualified grant of criminal jurisdiction over “all offenses against the laws of the United States.” Justice Kagan’s invocation of Samantar reinforces, rather than undermines, this reading: where FSIA does not apply by its terms, we may consider residual common-law/comity principles, but we should not expand a civil statute to create an implied categorical criminal-immunity bar. Verlinden and Amerada Hess’s “sole basis” language is best read—consistent with Roberts’s point—as confined to civil end-runs around FSIA, and extending it to criminal prosecutions would go beyond both precedent and text.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument remains that the FSIA was intended to be “comprehensive” and to embody background immunity principles traceable to The Schooner Exchange, but that cannot overcome the statute Congress actually enacted: repeated, deliberate limitation to “nonjury civil action[s]” and civil-process machinery. Chief Justice Roberts’s clear-statement point is decisive for me—reading a civil immunity statute to silently withdraw 18 U.S.C. § 3231’s unqualified criminal jurisdiction would be an implausible implied repeal with substantial practical consequences. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Samantar further supports a restrained approach: where FSIA does not apply by its terms, any residual comity/immunity questions are handled through common-law or Executive Branch tools, not by expanding FSIA beyond its text. Verlinden and Amerada Hess’s “sole basis” language arose in civil end-runs and should not be extended to create a categorical criminal-immunity regime absent clear statutory direction.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The petitioner’s best argument—grounded in The Schooner Exchange and the FSIA’s purported “comprehensiveness”—still cannot overcome the statute’s enacted limitation to “nonjury civil action[s]” and its exclusively civil procedural machinery. Chief Justice Roberts’s clear-statement point is decisive under a textualist approach: we should not infer that a civil immunity statute silently retracts 18 U.S.C. § 3231’s unqualified grant of jurisdiction over “all offenses against the laws of the United States.” Justice Kagan’s Samantar-based framing reinforces the proper analytic move: where the FSIA does not apply by its terms, we do not expand it; we consider any residual immunity or comity principles at common law, which cannot negate a direct jurisdictional grant absent congressional action. Verlinden and Amerada Hess, as several colleagues note, speak to FSIA exclusivity in the civil end-run context and do not supply a textual basis to bar criminal prosecutions.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The opposing side’s strongest contention remains that The Schooner Exchange’s background immunity presumption, combined with the FSIA’s “comprehensive/sole basis” language in Verlinden and Amerada Hess, should be read to bar criminal process absent a clear waiver. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, that “sole basis” framing arose in civil end-runs and the FSIA’s enacted text repeatedly and deliberately limits itself to “nonjury civil action[s]” and civil procedural machinery—an ill fit for silently withdrawing 18 U.S.C. § 3231’s unqualified criminal jurisdiction. Justice Kagan’s invocation of Samantar further supports treating non-FSIA immunity questions, if any, as residual common-law/comity matters rather than expanding the FSIA by implication to create a categorical criminal-immunity bar. Comity and fairness concerns are real (as Justice Sotomayor notes), but under a clear-statement and practical-consequences lens, they counsel calibrated procedural protections and Executive-branch tools, not a judge-made jurisdictional carveout.

John Roberts.reasoning: Section 3231 grants district courts jurisdiction over “all offenses against the laws of the United States,” and the FSIA’s text and structure—codified in Title 28 and focused on “civil action[s]” and civil removal—do not clearly strip that ordinary criminal jurisdiction or create a comprehensive criminal-immunity regime. While Halkbank invokes common-law sovereign immunity (The Schooner Exchange v. McFaddon), Congress in the FSIA principally displaced that common law in the civil context, and the absence of a clear statement extending immunity to criminal prosecutions counsels against reading such a limitation into § 3231. This narrower ground preserves institutional legitimacy by adhering to enacted text rather than expanding immunity by implication, while leaving to Congress the choice to add any express criminal-prosecution immunity for foreign-state instrumentalities. Weltover’s commercial-activity framework underscores that foreign instrumentalities can be treated as juridically distinct entities engaging in market conduct, reinforcing that generally applicable U.S. laws may reach such conduct when Congress has criminalized it with a U.S. nexus.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The FSIA’s text repeatedly and expressly cabins its jurisdictional and immunity regime to “any nonjury civil action,” 28 U.S.C. §§ 1330(a), 1604, and its accompanying procedures (e.g., removal of “[a]ny civil action,” § 1441(d)) likewise presuppose civil litigation rather than criminal prosecution. Reading the statute according to its ordinary public meaning in 1976, that deliberate civil-only phrasing does not silently withdraw the district courts’ preexisting criminal subject-matter jurisdiction conferred by 18 U.S.C. § 3231 over “all offenses against the laws of the United States.” Whatever common-law immunities may have existed under The Schooner Exchange, Congress in the FSIA chose a comprehensive civil scheme, and absent textual indication extending immunity to criminal cases, this Court should not add such a limitation by implication. Accordingly, § 3231 supplies subject-matter jurisdiction for the prosecution, and the FSIA does not bar it.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 3231 gives the district courts jurisdiction over “all offenses against the laws of the United States,” and nothing in the FSIA’s text purports to withdraw that ordinary criminal jurisdiction or to create immunity from federal criminal prosecution for agencies or instrumentalities. The FSIA’s provisions and structure—e.g., § 1330 (civil jurisdiction), § 1441(d) (removal of civil actions), and the service and execution sections—are tailored to “civil actions,” and Verlinden’s statement that the FSIA is the “sole basis” for jurisdiction applies in that civil context, not as an atextual bar on criminal enforcement. Extending FSIA immunity to criminal cases would require an additional clear statement that Congress did not enact and would invite serious practical consequences by creating a broad enforcement gap for generally applicable criminal statutes aimed at bank misconduct with a U.S. nexus. Whatever residual common-law comity concerns exist after the FSIA, they cannot override § 3231’s plain jurisdictional grant absent a statutory command.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: 18 U.S.C. § 3231 is an unqualified grant of subject-matter jurisdiction over “all offenses against the laws of the United States,” and nothing in the FSIA’s text purports to withdraw that criminal jurisdiction. The FSIA by its terms governs “nonjury civil action[s]” against a foreign state, 28 U.S.C. § 1330(a), and this Court has consistently described it as a civil scheme, including in Republic of Argentina v. NML Capital, Ltd., 573 U.S. 134, 141 (2014), rather than a general immunity bar across all proceedings. Consistent with In re Grand Jury, 912 F.3d 623, 628 (D.C. Cir. 2019), a state-owned bank engaged in commercial banking should not be categorically insulated from federal criminal law absent a clear statutory command, especially where prosecution can protect vulnerable communities from real-world harms tied to financial crime. Any comity concerns are better addressed through established doctrines and calibrated remedies rather than a judge-made expansion of immunity that would create an accountability gap.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 3231’s broad grant of criminal subject-matter jurisdiction (“all offenses against the laws of the United States”) comfortably covers indictments under generally applicable federal criminal statutes, and nothing in the FSIA’s text purports to withdraw that jurisdiction in criminal cases. The FSIA is structured around “civil action[s]” and a civil jurisdictional grant in 28 U.S.C. § 1330, and this Court’s statements treating the FSIA as “comprehensive” (e.g., Argentine Republic v. Amerada Hess Shipping Corp.) arose in civil efforts to bypass the FSIA’s civil immunity framework, not in criminal prosecutions. Samantar confirms that when the FSIA does not apply, immunity questions may be governed by common-law principles rather than by extending the FSIA beyond its terms; that makes it hard to infer a clear, FSIA-based bar to criminal prosecutions of state-owned instrumentalities absent textual direction. Given the strong workability concerns (e.g., obstruction of investigations) and the absence of a clear statement in the FSIA limiting § 3231, the better reading is that the district court retains jurisdiction, with any residual comity/immunity issues addressed through applicable common-law doctrines rather than a categorical jurisdictional bar.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Section 3231’s text grants district courts jurisdiction over “all offenses against the laws of the United States,” and nothing in the FSIA’s plain terms purports to withdraw that criminal jurisdiction. The FSIA repeatedly speaks in expressly civil terms—granting jurisdiction over “nonjury civil action[s]” in § 1330(a) and structuring immunity and exceptions around civil litigation—so, as a textual matter, it does not supply a clear bar to federal criminal prosecutions of a foreign state’s instrumentality. While petitioner invokes a background presumption of sovereign immunity rooted in cases like The Schooner Exchange, Congress in the FSIA codified a civil immunity regime without clearly extending it to criminal proceedings, and this Court’s exclusivity language in Verlinden and Amerada Hess is tied to “civil actions” against foreign states. Absent statutory text extending immunity to criminal cases, § 3231’s jurisdictional grant remains operative and the prosecution may proceed.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: 18 U.S.C. § 3231 is a broad, unqualified grant of subject-matter jurisdiction over “all offenses against the laws of the United States,” and the FSIA’s text and structure (28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1602–1611) are directed at civil “actions” and do not clearly purport to withdraw or limit that criminal jurisdiction. Under an institutional, precedent-focused approach, it is significant that this Court has repeatedly treated the FSIA as a comprehensive scheme for civil immunity and jurisdiction, while not extending it to criminal cases absent a clear statement from Congress, and the D.C. Circuit has likewise rejected a categorical immunity bar to federal criminal process against foreign sovereign entities. Moreover, the FSIA’s restrictive theory—turning on the nature of “commercial activity” rather than its purpose—confirms that state-owned instrumentalities engaged in ordinary banking and market conduct are not entitled to special insulation from generally applicable rules, a logic consistent with Weltover even if that case arose in the civil context. Practical workability and comity concerns are real, but they are better addressed through clear statutory limits or executive-branch tools rather than by judicially creating a criminal-immunity regime not found in the FSIA’s text.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The text of the FSIA repeatedly speaks in expressly civil terms—granting jurisdiction over a “nonjury civil action” in 28 U.S.C. § 1330(a) and providing immunity in that same civil-action framework—so its original public meaning does not naturally extend to criminal prosecutions. By contrast, 18 U.S.C. § 3231 is an unqualified grant of subject-matter jurisdiction over “all offenses against the laws of the United States,” which “applies directly” to a federal indictment and is “hard to imagine” as anything other than a clear jurisdictional grant. Nothing in the FSIA purports to withdraw that criminal jurisdiction, and this Court’s FSIA cases (e.g., Verlinden) describe the statute as governing civil suits, not criminal cases; any residual common-law immunity cannot override § 3231 absent a clear congressional limitation. Accordingly, the district court has subject-matter jurisdiction, and any immunity argument must find its footing in a statute that actually addresses criminal process.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: 18 U.S.C. § 3231 broadly grants district courts jurisdiction over “all offenses against the laws of the United States,” and the FSIA’s text and structure—28 U.S.C. §§ 1330, 1602–1611—are framed around civil “actions” and civil-process mechanisms, not criminal prosecutions. While The Schooner Exchange recognizes immunity as a comity-based background principle, Congress did not clearly codify a criminal immunity bar in the FSIA, and reading one in would create a judge-made, categorical limitation on federal criminal jurisdiction with significant practical consequences for enforcing generally applicable criminal laws. Consistent with In re Grand Jury, 912 F.3d 623 (D.C. Cir. 2019), I would hold that FSIA does not strip § 3231 jurisdiction in criminal cases, though procedural fairness requires careful attention to service, notice, and diplomatic/comity concerns in how process is executed against a foreign instrumentality.
